questions.question: What is the most common cause of palpable purpura in young adults with arthralgia?
questions.explanation: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is the most common cause of palpable purpura in young adults, characterized by IgA deposits in small vessels and frequent association with arthralgia.

questions.question: In IgA nephropathy with palpable purpura and arthralgias, what histological finding is characteristic?
questions.explanation: Mesangial proliferation with dominant IgA deposits is the hallmark finding of IgA nephropathy, which may accompany systemic IgA vasculitis.

questions.question: What first-line treatment is indicated for IgA vasculitis with active kidney involvement?
questions.explanation: Systemic glucocorticoids are the initial treatment in IgA vasculitis with active renal involvement, reducing inflammation and protecting renal function.

questions.question: What joint manifestation is typical in patients with IgA vasculitis?
options: Low back pain with morning stiffness
questions.explanation: Arthralgias, especially in the knees and ankles, are common in IgA vasculitis, without erosions or deformities, unlike other inflammatory arthropathies.

questions.question: What factor is associated with a worse prognosis in IgA nephropathy with Schönlein-Henoch syndrome?
questions.explanation: Persistent proteinuria greater than 1 g/day is a marker of poor renal prognosis, related to a higher risk of progression to chronic kidney disease.

questions.question: Which antibody is most frequently detected in IgA vasculitis?
questions.explanation: In IgA vasculitis, ANCAs are usually negative; The presence of anti-IgA antibodies is a common, although non-specific, immunological finding.

questions.question: Which finding in the urinary sediment is characteristic of IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Blood casts in the urinary sediment are a typical finding of IgA nephropathy, indicating active glomerular hematuria and mesangial proliferation.

questions.question: What pathophysiological mechanism explains the presence of blood casts in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Mesangial proliferation with IgA deposits produces glomerular injury that allows erythrocytes to pass into the tubule, forming blood casts in the sediment.

questions.question: What is the most common clinical presentation associated with blood casts in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: La hematuria macroscópica recurrente, típicamente tras infecciones respiratorias, es la manifestación clásica de la nefropatía por IgA y se asocia a cilindros hemáticos en sedimento.

questions.question: What complementary test confirms the diagnosis when blood casts are observed in sediment?
questions.explanation: Renal biopsy with immunofluorescence showing mesangial deposits of IgA is the diagnostic standard; Hematic casts only point to glomerulonephritis.

questions.question: What laboratory finding usually accompanies blood casts in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Elevation of serum IgA is observed in some patients with IgA nephropathy, while hypocomplementemia and anti-GBM correspond to other glomerulonephritis.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment for patients with IgA nephropathy and blood casts with persistent proteinuria?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the initial treatment to reduce proteinuria and protect kidney function; Corticosteroids are reserved for high-risk cases.

questions.question: What is the classic presentation of IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: IgA nephropathy typically manifests with episodes of recurrent macroscopic hematuria, frequently triggered by respiratory or gastrointestinal infections, more common in young adults.

questions.question: What factor most frequently triggers macroscopic hematuria in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Upper respiratory tract infections, typically viral, are the classic trigger of recurrent macroscopic hematuria in IgA nephropathy, unlike other glomerulopathies.

questions.question: What histological finding is characteristic of IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Immunofluorescence shows predominant mesangial deposits of IgA, often accompanied by C3, distinguishing IgA nephropathy from other glomerulonephritis.

questions.question: What is the first line of treatment in a patient with IgA nephropathy and proteinuria >1 g/day?
questions.explanation: Inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin system (ACEI or ARB) are the recommended initial treatment to reduce proteinuria and protect renal function in patients with IgA nephropathy.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of patients with IgA nephropathy have recurrent macroscopic hematuria?
questions.explanation: Recurrent macroscopic hematuria is observed in approximately one third of patients with IgA nephropathy, being more common in children and young adults than in the elderly.

questions.question: Which serum antibody is associated with the pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: IgA1 with deficient galactosylation is produced in excess and forms immune complexes that are deposited in the mesangium, triggering the glomerular lesion characteristic of the disease.

questions.question: What urinary finding is typical in IgA nephropathy after upper respiratory infection?
questions.explanation: Recurrent macroscopic hematuria, frequently synchronous with upper respiratory infections, is the classic presentation of IgA nephropathy. The other findings are not characteristic of this entity.

questions.question: What is the central pathophysiological mechanism in postinfectious IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: IgA nephropathy is characterized by IgA deposits in the glomerular mesangium, which activate complement and inflammatory cells. The other mechanisms correspond to other nephropathies or renal processes.

questions.question: Which upper respiratory infection is classically associated with exacerbation of IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Streptococcal pharyngitis is the upper respiratory infection typically associated with exacerbations of hematuria in IgA nephropathy. Other infections do not have this classic association.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment in patients with IgA nephropathy and persistent proteinuria >1 g/day?
questions.explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors) are the initial treatment to reduce proteinuria and protect kidney function. The other drugs are reserved for selected or unresponsive cases.

questions.question: ¿Qué hallazgo en biopsia renal confirma el diagnóstico de nefropatía por IgA?
questions.explanation: La inmunofluorescencia que muestra depósito mesangial dominante de IgA es el hallazgo diagnóstico clave. Los otros patrones corresponden a otras glomerulopatías o lesiones inespecíficas.

questions.question: What is the most feared long-term complication in untreated IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: La progresión a insuficiencia renal crónica es la complicación más grave y frecuente en la nefropatía por IgA, especialmente con proteinuria persistente. Las otras opciones son menos características o no definen el pronóstico.

questions.question: What laboratory finding typically characterizes IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: IgA nephropathy is associated with elevated serum IgA levels in approximately 50% of patients, although it is neither specific nor diagnostic on its own.

questions.question: What is the central pathophysiological mechanism in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: IgA nephropathy is characterized by predominant mesangial deposits of galactose-deficient IgA1, which triggers cell proliferation and expansion of the mesangial matrix.

questions.question: Which IgA predominates in the mesangial deposits of IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Mesangial deposits are mainly composed of IgA1, which is the predominant subclass in serum and shows aberrant galactose deficiency in this disease.

questions.question: Which IgA abnormality is associated with the pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Serum IgA1 in patients with IgA nephropathy presents galactose deficiency in the hinge region, which favors its recognition by antibodies and the formation of nephritogenic immune complexes.

questions.question: What is the diagnostic value of elevated serum IgA in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Elevation of serum IgA is a nonspecific finding and does not confirm the diagnosis, which requires renal biopsy with immunofluorescence that demonstrates dominant mesangial deposits of IgA.

questions.question: What other condition can present with elevated serum IgA simulating IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Henoch-Schönlein purpura, considered a systemic form of IgA nephropathy, also presents elevated IgA and mesangial IgA deposits, sharing similar pathogenic mechanisms.

questions.question: ¿Qué patrón histológico caracteriza a la nefropatía por IgA en su forma clásica?
questions.explanation: IgA nephropathy typically shows diffuse mesangial proliferation with IgA deposits in the mesangium, visible by immunofluorescence.

questions.question: What is the distinctive immunofluorescent finding in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Immunofluorescence reveals dominant IgA deposits in the mesangium, often accompanied by C3; this is pathognomonic of the disease.

questions.question: ¿Qué factor se asocia a exacerbación de hematuria en nefropatía por IgA?
questions.explanation: Respiratory or gastrointestinal infections can trigger recurrent gross hematuria, typical of IgA nephropathy.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el tratamiento de primera línea en nefropatía por IgA con proteinuria persistente?
options: Inhibidores de la ECA o ARA II
questions.explanation: Inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin system (ACEI or ARB) are the initial pillar to reduce proteinuria and delay progression in these patients.

questions.question: What finding indicates a poor prognosis in a biopsy of IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Glomerular sclerosis, interstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy predict progression to chronic renal failure, unlike mild changes.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el mecanismo fisiopatológico central en la nefropatía por IgA?
questions.explanation: La IgA1 con galactosilación deficiente forma complejos que se depositan en mesangio, activando complemento y células mesangiales, causando proliferación.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el hallazgo inmunopatológico característico en la nefropatía por IgA?
options: Depósitos lineales de IgG en membrana basal
Subepithelial deposits of C3 and IgG
Mesangial deposits of IgM and C1q
questions.explanation: IgA nephropathy is defined by the presence of IgA-dominant mesangial deposits, frequently accompanied by C3, detected by immunofluorescence. The other patterns correspond to other glomerulopathies.

questions.question: Which laboratory technique is essential to confirm mesangial IgA deposition?
questions.explanation: Direct immunofluorescence on the renal biopsy demonstrates mesangial IgA deposits, a necessary finding for diagnosis. Electron microscopy is supportive but not diagnostic by itself.

questions.question: What histological pattern is most frequently seen in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: The typical histological finding is mesangial expansion with hypercellularity, which can be focal or diffuse. Segmental glomerulosclerosis appears in advanced forms, not as an initial pattern.

questions.question: What serum molecule is associated with the pathogenesis of mesangial IgA deposits?
questions.explanation: IgA1 with aberrant galactosylation in the hinge region forms complexes that are deposited in the mesangium and activate the alternative complement pathway. IgA2, IgG4 or IgM do not participate in this mechanism.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment in patients with IgA nephropathy and proteinuria >1 g/day?
questions.explanation: Inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin system (ACEI or ARB) are the basis of treatment to reduce proteinuria and progression. Corticosteroids are reserved for selected cases after optimizing the antiproteinuric blockade.

questions.question: Which clinical finding is most suggestive of IgA nephropathy in a young patient?
questions.explanation: La hematuria macroscópica recurrente, a menudo tras infecciones respiratorias, es la presentación clásica en adultos jóvenes. El síndrome nefrótico puro o la hipertensión maligna no son los patrones iniciales típicos.

questions.question: ¿Qué hallazgo inmunopatológico distingue al síndrome de Goodpasture de la nefropatía por IgA en la biopsia renal?
options: Depósitos subepiteliales de IgG e IgA
Depósitos granulares de C3 en asas capilares
Depósitos lineales de IgG en membrana basal glomerular
questions.explanation: El síndrome de Goodpasture se caracteriza por anticuerpos anti-MBG que forman depósitos lineales de IgG a lo largo de la membrana basal glomerular, mientras que la nefropatía por IgA muestra depósitos mesangiales granulares de IgA.

questions.question: In a patient with glomerular hematuria and positive anti-GBM antibodies, what is the first-line treatment?
options: ACE inhibitors and low sodium diet
questions.explanation: Active Goodpasture syndrome requires plasmapheresis to remove anti-GBM antibodies along with cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids to suppress the production of new antibodies, unlike IgA nephropathy which is managed with blockade of the renin-angiotensin system.

questions.question: Which clinical manifestation is more characteristic of Goodpasture syndrome than of IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Goodpasture syndrome classically combines alveolar hemorrhage (hemoptysis) with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, while IgA nephropathy typically presents with recurrent macroscopic hematuria without pulmonary involvement.

questions.question: Which of the following antibodies is detected in Goodpasture syndrome?
questions.explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is associated with antibodies directed against the NC1 domain of type IV collagen of the glomerular and alveolar basal membrane, while the other antibodies correspond to ANCA vasculitis, lupus and membranous nephropathy respectively.

questions.question: Which chest x-ray finding would support the diagnosis of Goodpasture syndrome rather than IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage produces bilateral, often symmetrical, alveolar infiltrates on chest radiography. In IgA nephropathy there is no lung involvement; The other patterns are less specific or indicate other pathologies.

questions.question: What is the central pathophysiological mechanism of Goodpasture syndrome?
options: Deposition of mesangial IgA immune complexes
questions.explanation: El síndrome de Goodpasture es una enfermedad autoinmune mediada por anticuerpos IgG contra el colágeno tipo IV de la membrana basal, que causa glomerulonefritis y hemorragia alveolar. La nefropatía por IgA se debe a depósitos de IgA, y las otras opciones corresponden a otras entidades.

questions.question: What is the clinical factor most associated with rapid progression in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Persistent proteinuria greater than 1 g/day is a well-established independent risk factor for progression to renal failure in IgA nephropathy.

questions.question: What histological finding predicts a worse renal prognosis in Berger's disease?
questions.explanation: The presence of segmental sclerosis and glomerulosclerosis in the kidney biopsy indicates chronic and irreversible damage, being associated with a higher risk of progression to end-stage renal disease.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment to delay progression in patients with proteinuria >1 g/day?
questions.explanation: Inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin system (ACEI or ARB) are the basis of antiproteinuric and renoprotective treatment in IgA nephropathy with significant proteinuria.

questions.question: What criterion indicates initiation of immunosuppressive therapy in IgA nephropathy?
options: Persistent proteinuria >1 g despite ACEI/ARB II
questions.explanation: The indication for immunosuppression is reserved for patients with persistent proteinuria >1 g/day despite optimal blockade of the renin-angiotensin system and control of blood pressure.

questions.question: What is the central pathophysiological mechanism in the progression of IgA nephropathy?
options: Endothelial damage due to chronic hyperglycemia
Activation of the classical complement pathway
Deposit of IgA immune complexes in the mesangium
questions.explanation: The deposition of poorly galactosylated IgA1 immune complexes in the glomerular mesangium triggers cell proliferation and cytokine activation, being the initial event of kidney injury.

questions.question: What glomerular filtration rate indicates progression to stage 4 chronic kidney disease?
questions.explanation: Stage 4 of chronic kidney disease is defined by a glomerular filtration rate between 15 and 29 mL/min/1.73m2, which reflects a severe loss of kidney function and high risk of progression to dialysis.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of steroid therapy in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Steroid therapy in IgA nephropathy is mainly used to reduce proteinuria, which is associated with less progression to end-stage renal disease. Hematuria and creatinine are not the primary objectives of steroid treatment.

questions.question: In which patients with IgA nephropathy is it recommended to start steroids?
questions.explanation: The indication for steroids in IgA nephropathy is reserved for patients with persistent proteinuria greater than 1 g/day despite adequate blockade of the renin-angiotensin system, after 3-6 months of optimal treatment. Isolated hematuria or normal creatinine do not justify its use.

questions.question: Which steroid regimen is most recommended in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: The most commonly used regimen in IgA nephropathy is oral prednisone or intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone. The topical route is not useful in this glomerular disease. Intramuscular dexamethasone is not a standard regimen.

questions.question: What is the main adverse effect of prolonged steroid use in this disease?
questions.explanation: Si bien todos son efectos adversos posibles, las infecciones graves son el riesgo más temido y limitante del tratamiento esteroideo en la nefropatía por IgA, especialmente con dosis altas. Los otros efectos también ocurren pero no son tan frecuentes ni severos como las infecciones.

questions.question: Which recent study showed increased risk of adverse events with steroids in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Randomized clinical trials, such as STOP-IgAN and TESTING, have shown that steroid use is associated with an increased risk of serious adverse events, mainly infections, without a clear benefit on long-term renal survival in all patients.

questions.question: What is the optimal duration of steroid treatment in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: The optimal duration of steroid treatment in IgA nephropathy is not clearly defined, but most regimens use a duration of 6 months, as in the TESTING study, which evaluated oral methylprednisolone for 6 months. Longer treatments increase the risk of adverse effects without additional benefit.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of ACE inhibitors in IgA nephropathy?
options: Aumentar la excreción de sodio y agua
Reduce proteinuria and preserve kidney function
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors decrease intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, delaying the progression of chronic kidney disease in patients with IgA nephropathy.

questions.question: What hemodynamic effect explains the renoprotection of ACE inhibitors?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors produce preferential vasodilation of the efferent arteriole, reducing glomerular hydrostatic pressure and hyperfiltration, which reduces proteinuria and renal damage.

questions.question: What is the therapeutic objective when using ACE inhibitors in this nephropathy?
options: Reduce serum creatinine to normal values
questions.explanation: The objective is to reduce proteinuria to below 0.5 g/day, since higher levels are associated with greater progression to end-stage renal failure. The aim is not to normalize IgA or creatinine.

questions.question: What parameter requires adjustment of the dose of ACE inhibitors in these patients?
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia is a relevant adverse effect of ACE inhibitors; If potassium exceeds 5.5 mEq/L, the dose should be reduced or discontinued, also monitoring serum creatinine.

questions.question: When is it recommended to start ACE inhibitors in IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: The main indication is persistent proteinuria greater than 0.5 g/day, regardless of blood pressure, to offer renoprotection; Isolated hematuria does not justify the start.

questions.question: What additional measure is used if proteinuria persists despite the ACE inhibitor?
options: Asociar bloqueante del receptor de angiotensina
Increase the dose of oral corticosteroids
questions.explanation: If proteinuria is not controlled with the maximum tolerated dose of ACE inhibitor, an ARA II can be added to enhance the blockade of the renin-angiotensin system, always monitoring potassium and kidney function.

questions.question: What is the histological recurrence rate of IgA nephropathy in kidney transplantation at 10 years?
questions.explanation: Although clinical recurrence is variable, histological recurrence of IgA nephropathy in the kidney graft reaches approximately 50% at 10 years, being higher in young patients and with rapidly progressive disease.

questions.question: What factor is associated with a higher risk of recurrence of post-transplant IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Recurrence of IgA nephropathy is more common in young recipients, especially those with recurrent macroscopic hematuria or aggressive histology in the native. Advanced age and a cadaveric donor are not clear risk factors.

questions.question: Which histologic finding in the graft suggests recurrence of IgA nephropathy?
questions.explanation: Recurrence of IgA nephropathy is characterized by mesangial deposits of dominant or co-dominant IgA, similar to the native kidney. C4d indicates antibody-mediated rejection, thrombi suggest thrombotic microangiopathy, and infiltrate may be cellular rejection.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el tratamiento de primera línea para recurrencia sintomática de nefropatía por IgA en trasplante?
questions.explanation: El manejo inicial de la recurrencia de nefropatía por IgA se centra en control de proteinuria con bloqueo del sistema renina-angiotensina (IECA/ARA II) y optimización de la presión arterial. Los esteroides y recambio plasmático se reservan para casos graves o rápidamente progresivos.

questions.question: ¿Qué complicación se asocia a la recurrencia de nefropatía por IgA en el injerto?
questions.explanation: Recurrence of IgA nephropathy can cause graft loss, although it is less common than loss due to chronic rejection. Nephrotoxicity due to calcineurin inhibitors and acute rejection are causes of graft dysfunction not directly related to recurrence.

questions.question: What strategy reduces the risk of recurrence of IgA nephropathy in transplantation?
options: Use of HLA identical living donor
questions.explanation: Transplantation from a cadaveric donor is associated with a lower risk of recurrence of IgA nephropathy compared to a living donor, possibly due to lower immunogenicity or differences in the immunological response. There is no evidence that delaying transplant reduces the risk.
